label: Endocrine
blurb: Diabetes agents, thyroid drugs, corticosteroids, bone and pituitary therapy

drugs.name: Metformin
drugs.primaryEffect: Lowers blood glucose without causing hypoglycemia
drugs.treatmentUsage: First-line therapy for type 2 diabetes mellitus, prediabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome with insulin resistance
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Activates AMP-activated protein kinase, decreasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and increasing peripheral insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake.
drugs.sideEffects: Diarrhea and abdominal discomfort, metallic taste, vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use, lactic acidosis (rare but serious), weight neutrality or modest loss
drugs.contraindications: eGFR below 30 mL/min, acute or unstable heart failure, severe hepatic impairment, alcohol abuse, hold before iodinated contrast if renal function is impaired
drugs.tooltip: First-line for type 2 diabetes because it lowers A1c well, causes no hypoglycemia alone, and does not cause weight gain. Watch for B12 deficiency and hold it around contrast studies.

drugs.name: Glipizide
drugs.primaryEffect: Stimulates insulin release from pancreatic beta cells
drugs.treatmentUsage: Type 2 diabetes mellitus when additional glucose lowering is needed and cost is a concern
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the SUR1 subunit and closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells, causing depolarization, calcium influx, and insulin exocytosis independent of glucose level.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia (the main risk), weight gain, rash, hyponatremia, disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol in some agents
drugs.contraindications: Type 1 diabetes, sulfa allergy, severe renal or hepatic impairment; caution in the elderly and in irregular eaters
drugs.tooltip: Because insulin release is glucose-independent, sulfonylureas cause true hypoglycemia. Preferred over glyburide in older adults and renal impairment because its metabolites are inactive.

drugs.name: Sitagliptin
drugs.primaryEffect: Modestly lowers glucose by prolonging incretin action
drugs.treatmentUsage: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, typically as add-on therapy to metformin
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits dipeptidyl peptidase-4, the enzyme that degrades GLP-1 and GIP, so endogenous incretin levels rise and glucose-dependent insulin secretion increases while glucagon falls.
drugs.sideEffects: Nasopharyngitis, headache, pancreatitis, severe joint pain, bullous pemphigoid, heart failure hospitalization with some agents in the class
drugs.contraindications: History of pancreatitis; requires renal dose adjustment; concurrent GLP-1 agonist is redundant
drugs.tooltip: Weight neutral with no hypoglycemia because the incretin effect is glucose-dependent, but A1c lowering is modest. Bullous pemphigoid and arthralgia are the distinctive adverse effects.

drugs.name: Semaglutide
drugs.primaryEffect: Lowers glucose while producing substantial weight loss
drugs.treatmentUsage: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic weight management, cardiovascular risk reduction in type 2 diabetes
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Agonizes GLP-1 receptors to increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon, delay gastric emptying, and increase hypothalamic satiety signaling.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, pancreatitis, gallstones, delayed gastric emptying with aspiration risk under anesthesia, medullary thyroid carcinoma in rodents
drugs.contraindications: Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2 (boxed warning), history of pancreatitis, gastroparesis
drugs.tooltip: GLP-1 agonists lower A1c, cause major weight loss, and reduce cardiovascular events. The boxed warning for medullary thyroid carcinoma comes from rodent C-cell tumors and drives the contraindications.

drugs.name: Empagliflozin
drugs.primaryEffect: Lowers glucose by causing urinary glucose excretion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Type 2 diabetes, heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease progression
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 in the proximal tubule, blocking roughly 90 percent of filtered glucose reabsorption and producing glycosuria and osmotic diuresis.
drugs.sideEffects: Genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infections, volume depletion and hypotension, euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, Fournier gangrene rarely
drugs.contraindications: Type 1 diabetes, dialysis, recurrent genital infections; hold before major surgery to avoid euglycemic ketoacidosis
drugs.tooltip: Now used as much for heart failure and kidney protection as for glucose. The high-yield adverse effect is euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, where ketosis occurs at near-normal glucose levels.

drugs.name: Pioglitazone
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases peripheral insulin sensitivity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, insulin resistance syndromes
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Agonist at the nuclear receptor PPAR-gamma, altering transcription of genes that increase adipocyte glucose uptake, promote fatty acid storage, and improve insulin sensitivity.
drugs.sideEffects: Fluid retention and peripheral edema, weight gain, heart failure exacerbation, fractures in women, bladder cancer signal, hepatotoxicity
drugs.contraindications: Class III or IV heart failure (boxed warning), active bladder cancer, active liver disease
drugs.tooltip: It genuinely reverses insulin resistance and helps steatohepatitis, but fluid retention causing heart failure decompensation limits use. Onset of effect takes weeks because it works through gene transcription.

drugs.name: Insulin Lispro
drugs.primaryEffect: Covers the glucose rise from a meal
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prandial coverage in type 1 and type 2 diabetes, insulin pumps, correction dosing, diabetic ketoacidosis by infusion
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Amino acid substitutions at positions B28 and B29 prevent hexamer formation, so absorption is rapid with onset in 15 minutes and duration of three to four hours.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia, weight gain, lipohypertrophy at injection sites, hypokalemia from intracellular potassium shift
drugs.contraindications: Hypoglycemia; requires careful timing relative to meals
drugs.tooltip: Rapid-acting analogs are engineered to resist hexamer formation, which is why they absorb faster than regular insulin. Give with the meal, not 30 minutes before as with regular insulin.

drugs.name: Insulin Glargine
drugs.primaryEffect: Provides flat basal insulin coverage for about 24 hours
drugs.treatmentUsage: Basal insulin in type 1 and type 2 diabetes
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Glycine substitution and two added arginines shift the isoelectric point so the insulin precipitates in subcutaneous tissue and dissolves slowly, giving a peakless profile.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia especially nocturnal, weight gain, injection site pain, lipohypertrophy
drugs.contraindications: Hypoglycemia; must never be given intravenously or mixed with other insulins in the same syringe
drugs.tooltip: The peakless profile mimics physiologic basal secretion and causes less nocturnal hypoglycemia than NPH. Because it depends on subcutaneous precipitation, it cannot be given intravenously.

drugs.name: Regular Insulin
drugs.primaryEffect: Lowers glucose and shifts potassium intracellularly
drugs.treatmentUsage: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state by continuous infusion, hyperkalemia, prandial coverage, intravenous use in hospital
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase, triggering GLUT4 translocation for glucose uptake and activating Na-K-ATPase to drive potassium into cells.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia, hypokalemia, weight gain, injection site reactions
drugs.contraindications: Hypoglycemia, untreated hypokalemia in diabetic ketoacidosis where potassium must be repleted first
drugs.tooltip: The only insulin that can be given intravenously, making it the agent for DKA and hyperkalemia. In DKA, potassium below 3.3 must be corrected before insulin or fatal hypokalemia follows.

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.primaryEffect: Rapidly raises blood glucose
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe hypoglycemia when the patient cannot take oral glucose; beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker overdose; esophageal foreign body relaxation
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Activates hepatic Gs-coupled glucagon receptors, raising cAMP to stimulate glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; the same cAMP rise bypasses blocked beta receptors in the heart.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea and vomiting, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, headache; ineffective if hepatic glycogen is depleted
drugs.contraindications: Pheochromocytoma, insulinoma; ineffective in starvation, adrenal insufficiency, or chronic alcohol use with depleted glycogen
drugs.tooltip: The antidote for beta-blocker overdose because it raises cardiac cAMP without needing the beta receptor. It fails in hypoglycemia when glycogen stores are depleted, as in alcoholics.

drugs.name: Levothyroxine
drugs.primaryEffect: Replaces deficient thyroid hormone
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hypothyroidism of any cause, myxedema coma, TSH suppression in thyroid cancer, congenital hypothyroidism
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Synthetic T4 that is deiodinated peripherally to the active T3, which binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors and regulates transcription of genes governing metabolic rate.
drugs.sideEffects: Symptoms of hyperthyroidism if overdosed including palpitations, tremor, weight loss, atrial fibrillation, and accelerated osteoporosis; angina in coronary disease
drugs.contraindications: Untreated adrenal insufficiency because it can precipitate adrenal crisis; recent myocardial infarction; thyrotoxicosis
drugs.tooltip: Take on an empty stomach; calcium, iron, and PPIs block absorption. In elderly or coronary patients start low and go slow. Always treat adrenal insufficiency first to avoid precipitating crisis.

drugs.name: Methimazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces synthesis of new thyroid hormone
drugs.treatmentUsage: Graves disease and hyperthyroidism, preparation before thyroidectomy or radioiodine
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking oxidation of iodide, iodination of tyrosine residues, and coupling of iodotyrosines into T3 and T4.
drugs.sideEffects: Agranulocytosis, rash, arthralgia, hepatotoxicity of cholestatic type, aplasia cutis and other embryopathy in the first trimester
drugs.contraindications: First trimester of pregnancy, prior agranulocytosis with thionamides, severe hepatic disease
drugs.tooltip: Preferred over propylthiouracil except in the first trimester and thyroid storm. Any patient who develops fever or sore throat must stop the drug and have a white count checked for agranulocytosis.

drugs.name: Propylthiouracil
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hyperthyroidism in the first trimester of pregnancy, thyroid storm
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase to block hormone synthesis and additionally inhibits peripheral 5-prime-deiodinase, reducing conversion of T4 to the more active T3.
drugs.sideEffects: Severe hepatotoxicity and fulminant hepatic failure (boxed warning), agranulocytosis, ANCA-associated vasculitis, rash
drugs.contraindications: Routine first-line use because of hepatotoxicity; use limited to first trimester and thyroid storm
drugs.tooltip: Two niches only: first trimester (methimazole is teratogenic) and thyroid storm (it also blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion). Otherwise avoided because of fulminant hepatic failure risk.

drugs.name: Radioactive Iodine (I-131)
drugs.primaryEffect: Permanently ablates overactive thyroid tissue
drugs.treatmentUsage: Definitive treatment of Graves disease and toxic nodular goiter; ablation of residual thyroid cancer
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Concentrated by the sodium-iodide symporter in thyroid follicular cells, where beta emission destroys the surrounding tissue over weeks to months.
drugs.sideEffects: Permanent hypothyroidism (the expected outcome), transient thyroiditis with neck pain, worsening of Graves ophthalmopathy, sialadenitis
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy and breastfeeding (absolute), moderate to severe Graves ophthalmopathy, inability to follow radiation precautions
drugs.tooltip: Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because fetal thyroid is ablated after 10 weeks. It can worsen Graves eye disease, so ophthalmopathy patients get steroids or a different treatment.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.primaryEffect: Replaces physiologic glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Adrenal insufficiency, adrenal crisis, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, septic shock with vasopressor dependence
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Identical to endogenous cortisol, binding glucocorticoid receptors to regulate metabolism and inflammation and mineralocorticoid receptors to promote sodium retention.
drugs.sideEffects: Hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypokalemia, osteoporosis, immunosuppression, poor wound healing, Cushingoid features with excess
drugs.contraindications: Systemic fungal infection; never abruptly discontinue after prolonged therapy
drugs.tooltip: The replacement steroid of choice because its mineralocorticoid activity matches physiology. Doses must be tripled during illness — sick day rules — to prevent adrenal crisis.

drugs.name: Fludrocortisone
drugs.primaryEffect: Promotes sodium retention and potassium excretion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Primary adrenal insufficiency, salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Potent mineralocorticoid receptor agonist in the distal nephron that increases epithelial sodium channel and Na-K-ATPase activity, expanding volume and excreting potassium and hydrogen.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, heart failure exacerbation, hyperglycemia
drugs.contraindications: Systemic fungal infection, heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension
drugs.tooltip: Added to hydrocortisone in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency, because aldosterone production is preserved when the defect is pituitary. Monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renin.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.primaryEffect: Potent glucocorticoid effect with essentially no mineralocorticoid activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Cerebral edema, bacterial meningitis adjunct, croup, antenatal fetal lung maturation, chemotherapy-induced nausea, dexamethasone suppression testing, severe COVID-19
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds glucocorticoid receptors with very high affinity and long duration, suppressing NF-kB-driven inflammatory gene transcription and reducing capillary permeability.
drugs.sideEffects: Hyperglycemia, insomnia and mood changes, immunosuppression, myopathy, avascular necrosis, adrenal suppression, gastritis
drugs.contraindications: Systemic fungal infection, live vaccines; avoid abrupt withdrawal after prolonged use
drugs.tooltip: The steroid for cerebral edema and for testing the HPA axis, because it does not cross-react with cortisol assays. Given before or with the first antibiotic dose in pneumococcal meningitis.

drugs.name: Ketoconazole
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks adrenal cortisol synthesis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Medical management of Cushing syndrome when surgery is not possible; historically an antifungal
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits multiple cytochrome P450 steroidogenic enzymes including 17,20-lyase and 11-beta-hydroxylase, reducing cortisol and androgen synthesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Hepatotoxicity, gynecomastia and decreased libido from androgen blockade, QT prolongation, adrenal insufficiency, extensive CYP3A4 inhibition
drugs.contraindications: Hepatic disease, concurrent QT-prolonging drugs, coadministration with CYP3A4-dependent drugs
drugs.tooltip: Its antiandrogen effect causing gynecomastia is the classic Step 1 association. As a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor it also raises levels of many co-prescribed drugs dramatically.

drugs.name: Spironolactone
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks aldosterone and androgen receptor effects
drugs.treatmentUsage: Primary hyperaldosteronism, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, resistant hypertension, ascites from cirrhosis, hirsutism in PCOS, acne
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively antagonizes the mineralocorticoid receptor in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion; it also blocks androgen receptors and inhibits androgen synthesis.
drugs.sideEffects: Hyperkalemia, gynecomastia and breast tenderness, menstrual irregularity, metabolic acidosis, decreased libido
drugs.contraindications: Hyperkalemia, severe renal impairment, Addison disease, concurrent potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics
drugs.tooltip: The antiandrogen activity is a side effect in men (gynecomastia) and the therapeutic goal in women (hirsutism and acne in PCOS). Eplerenone is the selective alternative without endocrine effects.

drugs.name: Desmopressin
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases renal water reabsorption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Central diabetes insipidus, nocturnal enuresis, von Willebrand disease and mild hemophilia A, uremic bleeding
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Selective V2 receptor agonist that inserts aquaporin-2 channels into the collecting duct apical membrane, concentrating urine; V2 stimulation also releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelium.
drugs.sideEffects: Hyponatremia and water intoxication with seizures, headache, facial flushing, nausea; tachyphylaxis with repeated hemostatic dosing
drugs.contraindications: Hyponatremia, severe renal impairment, primary polydipsia, heart failure
drugs.tooltip: Selectivity for V2 over V1 means water retention without vasoconstriction. The water deprivation test distinguishes central DI, which responds to desmopressin, from nephrogenic DI, which does not.

drugs.name: Tolvaptan
drugs.primaryEffect: Produces free water excretion and raises serum sodium
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hypervolemic and euvolemic hyponatremia including SIADH; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease progression
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively blocks V2 receptors in the collecting duct, preventing aquaporin-2 insertion so free water is excreted without sodium loss, an effect called aquaresis.
drugs.sideEffects: Thirst, dry mouth, polyuria, hepatotoxicity, overly rapid sodium correction with osmotic demyelination risk
drugs.contraindications: Hypovolemic hyponatremia, inability to sense thirst, anuria, concurrent strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; must be initiated in hospital
drugs.tooltip: Must be started in hospital because sodium can rise too fast and cause osmotic demyelination syndrome. Correction should not exceed roughly 8 mEq/L in 24 hours.

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.primaryEffect: Broadly suppresses hormone secretion and splanchnic blood flow
drugs.treatmentUsage: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma and other neuroendocrine tumors, acute variceal bleeding, refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Long-acting somatostatin analog that binds somatostatin receptors 2 and 5, inhibiting release of growth hormone, insulin, glucagon, gastrin, VIP, and serotonin.
drugs.sideEffects: Gallstones and biliary sludge, steatorrhea, abdominal cramping, hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, bradycardia, vitamin B12 deficiency
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; caution in diabetes and gallbladder disease
drugs.tooltip: Somatostatin is the universal inhibitor, so octreotide suppresses nearly every gut and pituitary hormone. Gallstones occur in a large minority because gallbladder contraction is inhibited.

drugs.name: Cabergoline
drugs.primaryEffect: Suppresses prolactin secretion and shrinks prolactinomas
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prolactinoma and hyperprolactinemia (first-line), acromegaly as adjunct, Parkinson disease historically
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Potent D2 receptor agonist on pituitary lactotrophs, mimicking the tonic dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin release and reducing tumor size.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, headache, cardiac valvular fibrosis at high doses, impulse control disorders, psychosis
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, cardiac valvulopathy, history of pulmonary or retroperitoneal fibrosis
drugs.tooltip: Medical therapy is first-line for prolactinoma even with large tumors, because dopamine agonists shrink them dramatically. Antipsychotics, which block D2, are a common cause of drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

drugs.name: Alendronate
drugs.primaryEffect: Inhibits bone resorption and increases bone density
drugs.treatmentUsage: Osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, Paget disease of bone, hypercalcemia of malignancy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds hydroxyapatite and is taken up by osteoclasts, where it inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, disrupting the cytoskeleton and inducing osteoclast apoptosis.
drugs.sideEffects: Esophagitis and esophageal ulceration, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fractures, hypocalcemia, musculoskeletal pain
drugs.contraindications: Esophageal stricture or achalasia, inability to sit upright for 30 minutes, hypocalcemia, creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min
drugs.tooltip: Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water and remain upright for 30 minutes to prevent esophagitis. Correct vitamin D and calcium first, since bisphosphonates can cause hypocalcemia.

drugs.name: Denosumab
drugs.primaryEffect: Potently suppresses osteoclast formation and activity
drugs.treatmentUsage: Osteoporosis at high fracture risk, bone metastases and skeletal-related events, giant cell tumor of bone, hypercalcemia of malignancy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Monoclonal antibody against RANK ligand that prevents RANKL from binding RANK on osteoclast precursors, mimicking endogenous osteoprotegerin and blocking osteoclast differentiation.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypocalcemia, osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fracture, infection risk, severe rebound vertebral fractures if stopped without transition therapy
drugs.contraindications: Hypocalcemia (must be corrected first), pregnancy; never discontinue without transitioning to a bisphosphonate
drugs.tooltip: Safe in renal impairment unlike bisphosphonates, but stopping it causes a rebound in bone turnover with multiple vertebral fractures, so a bisphosphonate must follow.

drugs.name: Teriparatide
drugs.primaryEffect: Stimulates new bone formation rather than blocking resorption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Severe osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, failure of antiresorptive therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Recombinant PTH fragment 1-34 given as an intermittent daily injection, which preferentially stimulates osteoblast activity, whereas continuous PTH elevation stimulates resorption.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypercalcemia, orthostatic hypotension after injection, nausea, leg cramps, osteosarcoma in rats, injection site reactions
drugs.contraindications: Prior skeletal radiation, Paget disease, unexplained alkaline phosphatase elevation, hypercalcemia, open epiphyses
drugs.tooltip: The paradox is central: pulsatile PTH builds bone while continuous PTH (as in hyperparathyroidism) destroys it. Treatment is limited to two years and must be followed by an antiresorptive.

drugs.name: Cinacalcet
drugs.primaryEffect: Lowers parathyroid hormone and serum calcium
drugs.treatmentUsage: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in dialysis patients, parathyroid carcinoma, primary hyperparathyroidism when surgery is not possible
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Allosterically increases the sensitivity of the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor to extracellular calcium, so the gland perceives higher calcium and suppresses PTH secretion.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypocalcemia with paresthesias and tetany, nausea and vomiting, QT prolongation from hypocalcemia, adynamic bone disease
drugs.contraindications: Serum calcium below the normal range; requires close calcium monitoring
drugs.tooltip: It tricks the parathyroid into thinking calcium is high. Contrast with familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, where an inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation does the opposite.

drugs.name: Calcitriol
drugs.primaryEffect: Increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Chronic kidney disease-mineral bone disorder, hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D-dependent rickets, refractory hypocalcemia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: The fully activated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor, increasing transcription of intestinal calcium transport proteins and suppressing PTH gene expression.
drugs.sideEffects: Hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, nephrocalcinosis, vascular calcification, nausea and constipation
drugs.contraindications: Hypercalcemia, vitamin D toxicity, hyperphosphatemia without a phosphate binder
drugs.tooltip: Used when the kidney cannot perform 1-alpha-hydroxylation, as in chronic kidney disease or 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency. Plain cholecalciferol will not work in those settings.

drugs.name: Estradiol
drugs.primaryEffect: Replaces estrogen and relieves menopausal symptoms
drugs.treatmentUsage: Vasomotor symptoms of menopause, genitourinary syndrome of menopause, hypoestrogenism, primary ovarian insufficiency, gender-affirming therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds nuclear estrogen receptors alpha and beta, altering gene transcription in reproductive tissue, bone, vasculature, and the central thermoregulatory center.
drugs.sideEffects: Venous thromboembolism, stroke, endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma if unopposed, breast tenderness, gallbladder disease, hypertriglyceridemia
drugs.contraindications: History of estrogen-dependent cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, venous thromboembolism, active liver disease, smokers over 35
drugs.tooltip: Unopposed estrogen causes endometrial carcinoma, so a progestin must be added in any woman with a uterus. Thromboembolic risk is the main safety limitation.

drugs.name: Raloxifene
drugs.primaryEffect: Estrogen agonist in bone and antagonist in breast
drugs.treatmentUsage: Postmenopausal osteoporosis, breast cancer risk reduction in high-risk women
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds estrogen receptors and recruits different coactivators or corepressors depending on tissue, producing agonism in bone and antagonism in breast and uterus.
drugs.sideEffects: Hot flashes, leg cramps, venous thromboembolism, fatal stroke in women at cardiovascular risk
drugs.contraindications: History of venous thromboembolism, pregnancy, prolonged immobilization
drugs.tooltip: Contrast the SERMs: raloxifene is antagonist in both breast and uterus, while tamoxifen is antagonist in breast but agonist in uterus and therefore raises endometrial cancer risk.

drugs.name: Testosterone
drugs.primaryEffect: Restores androgenic and anabolic effects
drugs.treatmentUsage: Male hypogonadism, delayed puberty, gender-affirming therapy
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Binds the androgen receptor directly and after conversion to dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha-reductase; it is also aromatized to estradiol in peripheral tissue.
drugs.sideEffects: Polycythemia, acne, suppression of spermatogenesis and testicular atrophy, gynecomastia from aromatization, sleep apnea, prostate growth, dyslipidemia
drugs.contraindications: Prostate or breast cancer, desire for fertility, untreated severe sleep apnea, erythrocytosis, pregnancy exposure through skin contact
drugs.tooltip: Exogenous testosterone suppresses LH and FSH, which shrinks the testes and stops sperm production — the key counseling point for men who want children. Monitor hematocrit and PSA.

drugs.name: Finasteride
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces dihydrotestosterone levels
drugs.treatmentUsage: Benign prostatic hyperplasia, androgenetic alopecia
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase type 2, blocking conversion of testosterone to the far more potent dihydrotestosterone that drives prostate growth and follicular miniaturization.
drugs.sideEffects: Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia, decreased ejaculate volume, reduced PSA by about half, depression
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy and women of childbearing potential because of male fetal genital abnormalities; handling crushed tablets
drugs.tooltip: It halves PSA, so PSA values must be doubled when screening men on finasteride. Prostate shrinkage takes six months, unlike alpha-blockers which relieve symptoms within days.

drugs.name: Clomiphene
drugs.primaryEffect: Induces ovulation by increasing gonadotropin release
drugs.treatmentUsage: Ovulation induction in anovulatory infertility, especially polycystic ovary syndrome
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Antagonizes hypothalamic estrogen receptors, blocking negative feedback so GnRH pulse frequency rises, increasing FSH and LH and stimulating follicular development.
drugs.sideEffects: Hot flashes, ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, multiple gestation, visual disturbances, ovarian cysts, mood changes
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, ovarian cysts not from polycystic ovaries, liver disease, undiagnosed abnormal uterine bleeding
drugs.tooltip: It works by fooling the hypothalamus into perceiving low estrogen, which raises FSH. Letrozole has largely surpassed it in PCOS with higher live birth rates.

drugs.name: Leuprolide
drugs.primaryEffect: Initially stimulates then profoundly suppresses gonadotropins
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, central precocious puberty, gender-affirming puberty suppression
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Continuous GnRH receptor stimulation downregulates and desensitizes pituitary gonadotrophs after an initial flare, shutting off LH, FSH, and sex hormone production.
drugs.sideEffects: Initial tumor flare with worsening bone pain or urinary obstruction, hot flashes, decreased bone density, decreased libido, mood changes
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding; requires antiandrogen coverage during the initial flare in prostate cancer
drugs.tooltip: Pulsatile GnRH stimulates while continuous GnRH suppresses — that pharmacologic principle is the heart of the exam question. Cover the initial testosterone flare with an antiandrogen.

drugs.name: Somatropin
drugs.primaryEffect: Stimulates linear growth and anabolic metabolism
drugs.treatmentUsage: Growth hormone deficiency in children and adults, Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, chronic kidney disease-related growth failure, short bowel syndrome
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Recombinant human growth hormone that binds the GH receptor to stimulate hepatic IGF-1 production, which drives epiphyseal growth plate chondrocyte proliferation.
drugs.sideEffects: Insulin resistance and hyperglycemia, intracranial hypertension, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression, edema, arthralgias
drugs.contraindications: Closed epiphyses when used for height, active malignancy, acute critical illness, severe obesity in Prader-Willi with sleep apnea, proliferative retinopathy
drugs.tooltip: Growth hormone acts largely through hepatic IGF-1, so IGF-1 is used to monitor therapy. In Laron syndrome the receptor is defective, so GH is high, IGF-1 is low, and only IGF-1 therapy works.

drugs.name: Propranolol (Thyroid Storm)
drugs.primaryEffect: Rapidly controls the adrenergic manifestations of thyrotoxicosis
drugs.treatmentUsage: Thyroid storm, symptomatic hyperthyroidism, thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors to control tachycardia and tremor, and at high doses inhibits peripheral 5-prime-deiodinase conversion of T4 to T3.
drugs.sideEffects: Bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, fatigue, masking of hypoglycemia, heart failure exacerbation
drugs.contraindications: Asthma, decompensated heart failure, high-grade AV block, severe bradycardia
drugs.tooltip: The first drug given in thyroid storm because symptoms are largely adrenergic. Its inhibition of peripheral T4 to T3 conversion at high doses is a bonus that other beta-blockers lack.

drugs.name: Sevelamer
drugs.primaryEffect: Reduces intestinal phosphate absorption
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease and dialysis patients
drugs.mechanismOfAction: A nonabsorbed polymer that binds dietary phosphate in the gut lumen, forming an insoluble complex excreted in stool without delivering calcium or aluminum.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, constipation, bloating, metabolic acidosis, bowel obstruction rarely, reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
drugs.contraindications: Bowel obstruction, hypophosphatemia, dysphagia or severe gastrointestinal motility disorders
drugs.tooltip: Preferred over calcium-based binders because it avoids the calcium load that drives vascular calcification. It must be taken with meals to bind dietary phosphate.

drugs.name: Mifepristone
drugs.primaryEffect: Blocks cortisol and progesterone receptor signaling
drugs.treatmentUsage: Hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome; medical termination of pregnancy with misoprostol
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively antagonizes the glucocorticoid receptor, blocking cortisol action at the tissue level, and antagonizes progesterone receptors causing decidual breakdown.
drugs.sideEffects: Adrenal insufficiency that cannot be detected by cortisol levels, hypokalemia, endometrial thickening, vaginal bleeding, hypertension
drugs.contraindications: Pregnancy when used for Cushing syndrome, adrenal insufficiency, concurrent long-term corticosteroid therapy, ectopic pregnancy
drugs.tooltip: Because it blocks the receptor rather than lowering cortisol, cortisol levels rise and cannot be used to monitor therapy — adrenal insufficiency must be recognized clinically.

drugs.name: Acarbose
drugs.primaryEffect: Blunts the postprandial glucose spike
drugs.treatmentUsage: Type 2 diabetes with predominant postprandial hyperglycemia; prediabetes
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Competitively inhibits intestinal brush border alpha-glucosidases, delaying hydrolysis of complex carbohydrates into absorbable monosaccharides.
drugs.sideEffects: Flatulence, bloating, diarrhea from carbohydrate fermentation in the colon, elevated transaminases
drugs.contraindications: Inflammatory bowel disease, intestinal obstruction, cirrhosis, severe renal impairment
drugs.tooltip: A key testable point: hypoglycemia occurring while on acarbose must be treated with pure glucose, not sucrose or complex carbohydrates, because their breakdown is blocked.

drugs.name: Bromocriptine
drugs.primaryEffect: Suppresses prolactin and growth hormone secretion
drugs.treatmentUsage: Prolactinoma, acromegaly, type 2 diabetes, Parkinson disease, neuroleptic malignant syndrome
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Ergot-derived D2 receptor agonist that inhibits pituitary prolactin release and paradoxically suppresses growth hormone in acromegaly.
drugs.sideEffects: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, headache, nasal congestion, psychosis, erythromelalgia, retroperitoneal and valvular fibrosis
drugs.contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, cardiac valvulopathy, concurrent ergot alkaloids
drugs.tooltip: Largely replaced by cabergoline, which is better tolerated and dosed twice weekly. As an ergot derivative it carries fibrotic complications including cardiac valve disease.

drugs.name: Vasopressin
drugs.primaryEffect: Causes vasoconstriction and water retention
drugs.treatmentUsage: Septic and vasodilatory shock as a catecholamine-sparing vasopressor, cardiac arrest, diabetes insipidus, variceal hemorrhage
drugs.mechanismOfAction: Agonizes V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction through the phospholipase C pathway, and V2 receptors in the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 channels.
drugs.sideEffects: Digital and mesenteric ischemia, hyponatremia, myocardial ischemia, skin necrosis with extravasation, bradycardia
drugs.contraindications: Coronary artery disease with caution, peripheral vascular disease, hyponatremia
drugs.tooltip: In septic shock it is added to norepinephrine because vasopressin levels are relatively deficient and its receptor pathway remains responsive when adrenergic receptors are downregulated by acidosis.
